bug_description.normalized: The staged witness is the exact 22-byte BSON blob `20 20 20 20 13 00 20 20 20 ff ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff ff df`. `basic_bson_parser::parse()` stores element type `0x13` after an empty element name, so `read_value()` enters the decimal128 case and materializes the remaining 16 bytes as `dec.low = 0x202020ffff202020`, `dec.high = 0xdfffff2020202020`. `read_value()` then allocates `char s[42]` even though `decimal128_to_chars()` documents an output requirement of `BSON_DECIMAL128_STRING` (`43`) characters. On this witness the scientific-format prefix `-1.036685655102410889429905128712604E` already consumes 37 bytes, so `snprintf(str_out, 6, "%+d", 6145)` writes `+6145\0` with the terminator landing at `s[42]` one byte past the array while the returned pointer still advances to `s + 42`. The parser forwards the in-bounds 42-byte view `-1.036685655102410889429905128712604E+6145` as `semantic_tag::float128`; `basic_bson_encoder::visit_string()` reparses that non-NUL-terminated span in `decimal128_from_chars()`, whose `sscanf(++str_read, "%d%n", ...)` consumes exponent `6145` by relying on the overflowed terminator. The reparse stores 34 digits, sets `radix_position = 33`, and subtracts it to obtain `exponent = 6112`. The high-exponent normalization loop increments `last_digit` from 33 to 34, but the guard only rejects `last_digit - first_digit > 34`, not `>= 34`, so the later low-part accumulation loop reaches `digits[34]`. Stage 01 reproduced `UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: runtime error: index 34 out of bounds for type 'uint16_t [34]'` at `include/jsoncons_ext/bson/bson_decimal128.hpp:802:34`. The staged `patch.diff` hardens only the `decimal128_to_chars()` scientific-exponent append / buffer-size obligation and does not modify the crashing `decimal128_from_chars()` guard.

source.description: First project statement that turns an attacker-controlled BSON byte into the active dispatch key. For the saved witness, it stores `0x13` and commits the parser to the decimal128 path that later formats and reparses the 16-byte payload.
source.value_from: The exact `poc` is `20 20 20 20 13 00 20 20 20 ff ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff ff df`. After `begin_document()` consumes the first four bytes as the document length and `read_e_name()` immediately sees the empty name terminator `0x00`, the fifth byte `0x13` is stored here as `decimal128_cd`.
source.note: Scored source step. This is the first project-side state that uniquely selects the vulnerable decimal128 round-trip path.

tainted_value_origin.description: Scientific-exponent append that creates the exact reparse bytes and the overflowed terminator consumed later. For this witness, the prefix has already advanced `str_out` to `s + 37`, so formatting exponent `6145` writes the in-bounds bytes `+6145` and places the terminating `\0` at `s[42]` one byte past `char s[42]`.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: Step 2's `decimal128_t dec` and step 3's caller-provided `char s[42]`. The vulnerable caller gives `decimal128_to_chars()` only 42 bytes even though the function is documented for 43, and this exact payload takes the scientific branch with `scientific_exponent == 6145`, so the returned pointer becomes `s + 42` while the only terminator for the exponent lands out of bounds.

root_cause.description: Off-by-one bounds check. After reparsing the overflow-terminated 42-byte float128 view, the function has stored 34 digits and reduced parsed exponent `6145` by `radix_position = 33` to `6112`; one normalization iteration increments `last_digit` from 33 to 34, but this guard only rejects values strictly greater than `34` even though `digits` has valid indices `0..33`.
root_cause.note: For the exact string `-1.036685655102410889429905128712604E+6145`, `first_digit == 0`, `last_digit` enters the loop as `33`, and `34 > 34` is false. The function therefore carries an impossible logical digit index into the final significand encoding loop.

sink.description: UBSan crash site. In the low-part accumulation loop, `d_idx` reaches `34` and this read dereferences `digits[34]`, one element past `uint16_t digits[34]`.
sink.note: The saved sanitizer trace reports `index 34 out of bounds for type 'uint16_t [34]'` at `include/jsoncons_ext/bson/bson_decimal128.hpp:802:34` in `jsoncons::bson::decimal128_from_chars`.

parser_admitted.description: After the parser stores type `0x13`, the next parse iteration dispatches into `read_value()` with `decimal128_cd`, which is the only BSON branch that formats the 16-byte payload into a float128 string and reparses it.

evidence_limitations: The staged vulnerable workspace in `gt_results/arvo_34814/_work/src/jsoncons` is at commit `72154479e9b9c6daa66a5339d69f49286e7bf650`, not the metadata's `f60d3f81a327e6f96265794f809cd50e18e9596c`. All lines and code snippets here are grounded to the staged source that Stage 01 actually compiled and crashed on.

The staged `patch.diff` only hardens `decimal128_to_chars()` around the scientific-exponent append when the 42-byte string exhausts `char s[42]` and the terminator would land at `s[42]`; it never touches the crashing `decimal128_from_chars()` lines. This GT therefore uses the patch only as supporting evidence for the formatter boundary on the witness path, not as proof of the later off-by-one root cause at line 699.

coarse_trace.summary: The BSON parser stores attacker byte `0x13` as the current element type and dispatches into the decimal128 value path after consuming an empty element name.

The decimal128 branch reads the 16-byte payload into `decimal128_t`, then calls `decimal128_to_chars()` with `char s[42]`; the scientific-format exponent append writes the exact 42-byte string `-1.036685655102410889429905128712604E+6145` and places the terminating `\0` one byte past `s`.

Because the parser emitted `semantic_tag::float128`, the encoder reparses that same 42-byte non-NUL-terminated view with `decimal128_from_chars()`, whose exponent parser later depends on the overflowed terminator.

The reparse stores 34 significand digits, uses `sscanf()` to read exponent `6145`, and subtracts `radix_position = 33` to obtain `6112`, so the high-exponent normalization loop increments `last_digit` to `34` while the `> max_digits` guard still passes.
The final low-part accumulation loop then iterates through `digits[19..34]` and line 802 reads `digits[34]`, matching the saved UBSan index-out-of-bounds report.

fine_trace.note: Source. The saved witness's fifth byte is `0x13`, so after `read_e_name()` consumes the empty cstring name, the parser stores `decimal128_cd` as the current element type. That dispatch key is what makes the next `read_value()` call enter the decimal128-specific round-trip path.
The decimal128 case reads the remaining 16 payload bytes `20 20 20 ff ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff ff df` and materializes them as `dec.low = 0x202020ffff202020` and `dec.high = 0xdfffff2020202020`.

fine_trace.code:
char s[bson::decimal128_limits::buf_size];
auto r = bson::decimal128_to_chars(s, s+sizeof(s), dec);
fine_trace.note: The caller allocates `char s[42]` and invokes `decimal128_to_chars(s, s+sizeof(s), dec)`. That buffer is one byte shorter than the callee's documented `BSON_DECIMAL128_STRING` requirement of 43 characters, so this exact witness leaves no spare byte for an in-bounds exponent terminator.

For this `dec`, scientific format is selected and the prefix `-1.036685655102410889429905128712604E` already occupies 37 bytes, so `str_out == s + 37` when `scientific_exponent == 6145`. `snprintf` writes `+6145\0`; the five exponent bytes fit at `s[37..41]`, the terminator lands at `s[42]` one byte past `char s[42]`, and the function returns with its output pointer at `s + 42`.

`read_value()` wraps the in-bounds range `[s, r.ptr)` as a 42-byte `basic_string_view` and forwards it with `semantic_tag::float128`. The exact bytes are `-1.036685655102410889429905128712604E+6145`, but the terminator from step 4 sits outside the declared view at `s[42]`.

The encoder receives step 5's 42-byte view as `sv` with `tag == semantic_tag::float128`, so the `case semantic_tag::float128` arm reparses that same non-NUL-terminated span with `decimal128_from_chars()` instead of serializing it as a normal text string.

Scanning `-1.036685655102410889429905128712604E+6145` stores the exact 34-digit significand `1036685655102410889429905128712604` into `digits[0..33]`. At the end of the significand, `ndigits_read = ndigits = ndigits_stored = 34`, `first_nonzero = 0`, and `radix_position = 33` because there are 33 digits after the decimal point.

`SSCANF(++str_read, "%d%n", ...)` parses the exponent text as `exponent = 6145` and advances `nread = 5` to the end of the 42-byte view. Because this call ignores the `last` pointer, that successful stop after `+6145` depends on the overflowed terminator written at `s[42]` in step 4.
Because step 7 stored exactly 34 digits and there are no trailing zeros to discard, the active significand window is initialized as `first_digit = 0`, `last_digit = 33`, `significant_digits = 34`.
The parsed exponent `6145` is corrected by the 33 fractional digits from step 7, yielding `exponent = 6112`.

Root cause. Since step 10 left `exponent = 6112`, this normalization loop runs once, increments `last_digit` from `33` to `34`, and then accepts it because the guard is `> 34` rather than `>= 34`. The loop leaves a one-past-end logical digit index for the final significand encoding.

Sink. With `last_digit - first_digit == 34`, the two-part encoding branch runs: the high-part loop consumes `digits[0..17]`, `significand_low = digits[18]`, and the final low-part accumulation loop iterates `d_idx` through `19..34`. On the last iteration this line reads `digits[34]`, which matches the saved UBSan report.

cross_validation.sink_matches_crash: Yes. The saved run reports `include/jsoncons_ext/bson/bson_decimal128.hpp:802:34` in `jsoncons::bson::decimal128_from_chars`, which is the exact sink above.
cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: N/A - the saved UBSan array-bounds report has no allocation or free context.
cross_validation.trace_consistent_with_stack: Yes. The saved project stack `decimal128_from_chars -> basic_bson_encoder::visit_string -> basic_json_visitor<char>::string_value -> basic_bson_parser::read_value -> basic_bson_parser::parse -> basic_bson_reader::read -> LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` matches fine-trace step 5's read-value handoff, step 6's encoder reparse arm, and steps 7 through 12 inside `decimal128_from_chars()`, with `basic_json_visitor<char>::string_value` left as ordinary call plumbing.
cross_validation.tainted_value_reaches_sink: Yes. Step 4 appends the exponent bytes and overflowed terminator to `s`, step 5 passes the resulting 42-byte `[s, r.ptr)` view to `visitor.string_value(..., semantic_tag::float128, ...)`, step 6 reparses that same `sv.data(), sv.size()` span, and steps 7 through 11 show how it produces the `digits[]` and `last_digit` state consumed by the crashing read at step 12.
cross_validation.patch_resolves_note: The staged patch only hardens `decimal128_to_chars()` sizing behavior around the scientific-exponent append and does not modify the off-by-one `> max_digits` guard that directly permits `digits[34]`.

poc.trigger: Feeding the saved 22-byte `poc` to `fuzz_bson_encoder` makes the BSON parser select one empty-name decimal128 element, format its 16-byte payload into `char s[42]` where the scientific-exponent append writes `+6145\0` and places the terminator at `s[42]`, pass the resulting 42-byte `float128` view to the encoder, and then crash in `decimal128_from_chars()` when that reparse parses exponent `6145`, lets `last_digit` reach `34`, and finally reads `digits[34]`.

format.name: Exact 22-byte BSON document with one empty-name decimal128 element
format.contract: The file must be this exact 22-byte witness: `20 20 20 20 13 00 20 20 20 ff ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff ff df`. Byte 4 must be BSON type `0x13` (`decimal128_cd`), byte 5 must be the empty element-name terminator `0x00`, and the final 16 payload bytes must stay exactly `20 20 20 ff ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff ff df`; with the staged `char s[42]` caller, that exact payload produces the 37-byte prefix `-1.036685655102410889429905128712604E`, then writes `+6145\0` at `s + 37`, leaving the terminator at `s[42]` and giving `decimal128_from_chars()` the same 42-byte view that later reaches `digits[34]`.
